claims.text: Pack cementation can form an aluminum oxide coating on a refractory high-entropy alloy.
An aluminum oxide coating formed through pack cementation can improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The treatment produces an aluminum oxide layer as the structural mediator.
The aluminum oxide layer is dense and continuous.
The aluminum oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion reduces oxidation and degradation of the alloy.
The coated alloy will have an oxidation rate at least 50% lower than that of the untreated alloy.
The proposed improvement applies at temperatures from 1000°C to 1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for exposures of 100 to 500 hours.
Coating effectiveness may depend on the composition of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
Coating effectiveness may depend on the pack-cementation process parameters.
A comparative oxidation test at 1100°C for 200 hours in an oxygen-rich atmosphere can compare the coated alloy against the untreated alloy using oxidation rate, scale thickness, and microstructure.
The hypothesis is falsified if the coated alloy's oxidation rate is not significantly lower than that of the untreated alloy after the specified test.

contradictions.description: The conditions require temperatures above 1000°C and exposure times exceeding 100 hours, whereas the boundary includes exactly 1000°C and exactly 100 hours.

The predicted outcome specifies at least a 50% oxidation-rate reduction, but the falsification rule only requires a statistically significant reduction. A significant reduction smaller than 50% would fail the quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
